context: Al-Jathiyah is Makkan and sits inside the run of surahs opening with Ha Mim. Its audience had settled on a position and stated it in a sentence: this life is all there is, we die and we live, and nothing finishes a man except the passing of time. Verse 24 quotes them saying exactly that.

The structure follows from the position. The surah does not open with the Hereafter, it opens with what those same people looked at daily: the sky and the earth, their own making, the animals spread across the ground, night giving way to day, rain reviving dead land, the turning of the winds. Each is called a sign, and each is addressed to a differently named audience, those who believe, those who are certain, those who reason, those who reflect. The argument is that evidence was never in short supply.
name_story: The name is taken from verse 28, where every nation is seen kneeling and called to its own record. The Arabic word describes people down on their knees, the posture of someone waiting on a verdict rather than someone praying. A surah that begins by quoting men who say only time destroys them is named for the moment those same men are on their knees while the record is read out.

movements.note: Heavens and earth, the creation of the reader himself, the creatures scattered over the ground, night and day, rain and wind. Set against all of it is the man who hears the verses recited and then persists in arrogance as though he never heard a word.

The sea is made to carry ships, and whatever is in the heavens and the earth is placed at people's disposal, all of it from Him. A hard instruction follows: tell the believers to forgive those who have no expectation of the days of Allah.

movements.h: Israel, and a road of your own
movements.note: The Children of Israel were given scripture, judgement, prophethood and clear proofs, and then differed out of rivalry once knowledge had reached them. The Prophet ﷺ is placed on a clear road and told to follow it rather than the inclinations of people who do not know.

Those who pile up evil are told they will not be handled like the believers. The man who takes his own desire as his god is described with hearing sealed and sight veiled, and the deniers are quoted saying that nothing destroys them but time.

The Hour arrives, each community is called to a record that speaks against it in truth, and the record turns out to have been transcribed while the deeds were being done. All greatness in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and the surah stops there.

themes.d: Naming dahr as the thing that kills men puts an impersonal process where a Lord belongs. The Qur'an answers by naming the One who gives life and takes it, and the same substitution is still made today in newer vocabulary.

themes.t: The signs are graded by the one looking
themes.d: The same sky is called a sign for those who reason, for those who are certain, for those who reflect, and for those who believe. The difference is located in the observer, not in the object.

Verse 23 does not describe an idol of stone or an inherited cult. It describes a man whose god is what he wants, and it treats the deafness that follows as the result of a choice rather than a defect he was born with.
The register is not compiled at the end from memory. Verse 29 says it was being transcribed as the deeds were done, which makes the Day a reading rather than an investigation.

heart: This is a short surah with a very fast descent. Eleven verses carry a reader from the sky above his head to a man who hears the words of Allah and keeps walking, and twenty more reach an entire nation on its knees. Recited without hurry, that pace is what does the work, since nothing in it is repeated for emphasis.

The verse people tend to carry away is the one about a man whose god is his own desire, because it does not describe a foreign practice. Its wording lets a reader notice how a preference hardens into a principle and then into a rule nobody is allowed to question. Set against it stands the instruction in verse 14 to forgive those who expect nothing from the days of Allah, which keeps the surah from becoming a complaint about other people.

passages.why: Believers are told to forgive those who have no expectation of the days of Allah. Commentators differ over whether this was later superseded by the verses on fighting or stands as guidance on absorbing insult, and the disagreement is old and unresolved.
The only place in the Qur'an where the word shari'ah occurs. It is used of a road laid out to be walked, and it is set directly against following the inclinations of those who do not know.

The god made of desire, and the claim that time is what destroys men. A hadith qudsi in Bukhari and Muslim forbids abusing time and gives the reason: the alternation of night and day is Allah's own doing.
Every nation kneeling, and a record that speaks in truth because it was written down as the deeds happened. This is the image the surah is named for.

connections.why: Al-Furqan carries almost the same sentence about the man who takes his desire as his god, and follows it with a question about who could possibly be made responsible for such a person. The two verses are best read side by side.

Al-Insan opens by asking whether a stretch of time passed over man when he was not a thing worth mentioning. Al-Jathiyah's deniers say time is what destroys them; the other surah reminds them that time is also what they came out of.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Jathiyah. The long lists that assign a named reward to every surah in order, most of them going back to a narration attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, are judged forged by hadith critics, and nothing from that material is used here. This surah's standing rests on its content, and it is worth noting that a hadith qudsi in Bukhari and Muslim takes up its subject directly by forbidding the abuse of time.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; the fabricated series attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b is excluded
